subject: ss-plastic-surgery
title: Extensor Tendon Zones, Mallet Finger, Boutonniere and Swan-Neck

steps.say: Extensor injuries are mapped by nine zones running from fingertip to forearm, with each zone predicting the deformity. Zone one crosses the DIP joint, zone three crosses the PIP joint, and zone five crosses the knuckle joint. Higher zones are moving proximally through metacarpal dorsum, retinaculum, forearm, and muscle belly.
steps.tx: **Extensor tendons** divide into **nine zones** from tip to forearm. **Zone I** overlies the **DIP joint**, **Zone II** the middle phalanx, **Zone III** the **PIP joint**, **Zone IV** the proximal phalanx, **Zone V** the MCP joint, **Zone VI** the metacarpal dorsum, **Zone VII** the carpal retinaculum, **Zone VIII** the distal forearm, and **Zone IX** the muscle belly.

The image shows a dorsal hand with color bands marking extensor zones from fingertip to forearm, including DIP, PIP, knuckle, retinaculum and muscle belly. These are **Verdan zones**, nine territories where **Zone I** sits at the tip and higher numbers move **proximal**. Zone number predicts deformity and guides splint or repair choice.
steps.say: The picture shows the back of the hand and forearm wrapped in colored bands from tip to muscle. It teaches the nine level map where the first zone is at the fingertip and later zones run toward the forearm. Knowing the zone tells you which joint will droop and what care to choose.

vis.alt: Dorsal hand with colored bands marking nine extensor zones to forearm shown.
vis.caption: Color mapped extensor zones from fingertip upward Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: A drooping fingertip that cannot straighten is announcing a zone one failure. The extensor tendon is rupturing or avulsing a bone flake from the distal phalanx base. The DIP joint is falling into involuntary flexion that active effort cannot overcome.
steps.tx: Zone I injury causes **mallet finger** when the tendon ruptures or avulses bone from the **distal phalanx** base. The result is involuntary **DIP joint flexion** that the patient cannot actively straighten. The drooping tip is declaring a **Zone I** extensor failure.

steps.say: Closed mallet injuries are healing without surgery when extension is never surrendered. Continuous splinting in full DIP extension is lasting six to eight weeks to let the tendon reattach. Four further weeks of night splinting are protecting the repair while daytime motion resumes.
steps.tx: Closed **mallet finger** needs continuous uninterrupted **DIP joint extension splinting** for **6 to 8 weeks**, then **4 weeks** of night splinting. Daytime motion resumes while nights stay protected. One flexion lapse during day wear is restarting the whole clock from day one.

steps.say: The central slip is balancing the whole extensor hood over the PIP joint. Its rupture is sinking the PIP into flexion while the DIP is compensating into hyperextension. The lateral bands are sliding volar to the joint axis and locking in the boutonniere posture.
steps.tx: Zone III **central slip** rupture gives **boutonniere deformity**: **PIP flexion** with compensatory **DIP hyperextension** as lateral bands sublux volarly. The PIP sinks while the DIP overextends. The **extensor hood** imbalance is fixing the finger in a permanent buttonhole posture that stiffens with time.

The image shows a side section of a finger with a torn central slip, bent middle joint and straight overextended tip, plus volar shifted side bands. This is **boutonniere deformity** from **central slip** rupture, pairing **PIP flexion** with DIP hyperextension. Sliding bands lock the buttonhole posture that stiffens over time.
steps.say: The picture shows the middle joint sunk down while the tip tilts back, with the central tendon torn and the side bands slipped downward. It teaches the buttonhole pattern after middle joint tendon failure. The middle bends while the tip over straightens, and delay lets stiffness set in.

vis.alt: Side finger section with torn central tendon bent middle joint and overextended tip shown.
vis.caption: Buttonhole finger posture after central tendon rupture Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Bedside testing is proving central slip integrity without any imaging. The patient is flexing the PIP ninety degrees over a table edge and extending the DIP against resistance. Weak PIP extension with a rigid DIP is confirming that the central slip has ruptured.
steps.tx: The **Elson test** checks **central slip integrity**: PIP flexed **90 degrees** over a table edge, then DIP extension against resistance. Weak PIP extension with rigid DIP extension confirms **central slip rupture**, with lateral bands doing all the work. A firm DIP means the slip is intact.

steps.say: Swan-neck posture is mirroring boutonniere with the joints reversed. The PIP is hyperextending while the DIP is flexing into a graceful but useless curve. Dorsal band subluxation, volar plate laxity, or terminal extensor rupture is driving the deformity.
steps.tx: **Swan-neck deformity** pairs **PIP hyperextension** with **DIP flexion**, the mirror of boutonniere. Causes include dorsal **lateral band subluxation**, **volar plate** laxity, or **terminal extensor** rupture. The graceful curve is hiding a finger that cannot grip or pinch with any force.

steps.say: The knuckle extensor is sliding sideways out of its central track. Zone five rupture is striking the middle finger extensor digitorum communis tendon classically. The tendon is dropping into the ulnar groove so the knuckle cannot extend and visibly snaps on flexion.
steps.tx: Zone V **sagittal band** rupture strikes the middle finger **extensor digitorum communis (EDC)** tendon. The tendon subluxes into the ulnar **intermetacarpal groove**, so the knuckle will not extend and snaps sideways on flexion. The **sagittal band** normally centers the tendon over bone.

rows: Snapping knuckle that will not extend

steps.say: Six tunnels under the wrist retinaculum are organising the extensors into compartments. The first compartment is carrying abductor pollicis longus with extensor pollicis brevis for thumb release. The third compartment is guiding extensor pollicis longus around its tubercle for thumb extension.
steps.tx: The **extensor retinaculum** at **Zone VII** forms **six dorsal compartments** walled by vertical septa. Compartment **1** carries APL with EPB, while compartment **3** carries **EPL** around Lister tubercle. Each **fibro-osseous** tunnel is keeping its tendons gliding smoothly over the wrist bones.

rows: APL with EPB for thumb abduction
